traveler: Jakob Fugger 'the Rich' (Jakob Fugger von der Lilie)
title: The Fondaco to the Chapel: Silver, Copper, and the Crown of the Romans
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Weaver's House and the Fondaco

stops.name: Augsburg, the tenth of eleven children
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deutsche Biographie (gnd118694022) and en.wikipedia give 6 March 1459, tenth of eleven children of Jakob Fugger the Elder and Barbara Baesinger. The father's death in 1469 is likewise attested and is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In the Free Imperial City of Augsburg a tenth child is born to Jakob Fugger the Elder and Barbara Bäsinger, in a house that has already crossed from the weavers' guild into the merchants'. The father deals in fustian, the cloth of cotton and linen that Swabia sells to half of Europe. He dies ten years later, leaving Barbara at the ledger and the boy to be disposed of as family surplus. The firm goes on trading under the widow's name, and the youngest of eleven children grows up in a house where the books are kept by his mother.
suggested_refs: The Fugger fustian trade of the 1450s and 1460s, the family's crossing from the weavers' guild to the merchants'

stops.name: Herrieden, the prebend that may never have been
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction and tradition. Older biographies place the boy in minor orders holding a prebend at the Herrieden collegiate foundation, some lodging him there as a resident canon until 1478. de.wikipedia reports that post-2009 research refutes the residency, because documents show him representing the family at Venice from 1473. Coordinate corrected to the town's own, 49.2331 / 10.4978; the first pass carried 49.1964 / 10.8879, roughly 30 km east. The 1469 date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: The youngest son of a merchant house is the son the house can spare, and the church is where such sons are put. Tradition sets the boy Jakob in minor orders at the collegiate foundation of Herrieden in Middle Franconia, holding a prebend, some accounts lodging him there as a resident canon into his nineteenth year. The documents do not cooperate. By 1473 he is in Venice on the firm's business, aged fourteen, which leaves the canonry no room to sit in. The prebend, if he ever held it, was income and not a vocation.
suggested_refs: The collegiate foundation of Herrieden and its prebends; the post-2009 documentary revision of the Fugger canonry

stops.name: Nuremberg, the death of the brother
stops.date_confidence: the death is attested: de.wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger', records brother Peter's death in 1473 at Nuremberg and Markus's in 1478 at Rome. The causal claim, that Peter's death redirected Jakob from church to counting house, is traditional and unattested. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: His brother Peter dies at Nuremberg, on the road of the firm's business, in a year when Markus is still in Rome at the papal chancery and Ulrich and Georg are holding Augsburg. A house with eleven children can afford to give one to God; a house that starts losing sons to the roads cannot. The story the family tells afterward is that Peter's death takes the youngest brother out of the church and puts him on a horse to Venice. Whether anyone said so aloud in 1473, no paper records.
suggested_refs: The Fugger factoring post at Nuremberg, established with the Venice post in 1473
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Venice, the Fondaco dei Tedeschi
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia and the Fugger Foundation both put him at Venice from age fourteen in 1473, trained through the Fondaco, resident for most of the period to 1487. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate inherited from the atlas's existing Venice pin beside the Fondaco.
stops.campa: At fourteen he is sent down to the German warehouse on the Grand Canal, the Fondaco dei Tedeschi, where the merchants of the Empire eat, sleep, store, and are taxed under one roof by a republic that prefers its foreigners contained. Here he learns double entry, the bill of exchange, the assay of credit, and the cotton and fustian trade. He is resident there for most of the years to 1487, going home to Augsburg and coming back down. Double entry is what he takes away from it, and he keeps his books that way for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The Fondaco dei Tedeschi on the Grand Canal, the Empire's regulated trading house in Venice
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Rome, the brother in the chancery
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deutsche Biographie states that by 1478 he had traveled to Venice and Rome for commercial purposes. The exact date within the period is unknown, defaulted to 1478-01-01. Markus's post in the papal supplications chancery from 1471 and his death at Rome in 1478 are from de.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Before he is twenty he has been to Rome as well as Venice, on the firm's account. His brother Markus has held a place in the papal chancery of supplications since 1471, a desk where every petition to the Curia passes and where every petition costs money to move. Markus dies in Rome in 1478. What the family keeps is the knowledge of how Roman money travels: which office takes it, which bank carries it north, what a dispensation is worth on the day. The Fuggers will still be moving Curial funds half a century later.
suggested_refs: The papal chancery of supplications, where Markus Fugger held a place from 1471

stops.name: Gastein, the loan that becomes a mine
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fugger Foundation dates mining operations in the Gastein and Schladming areas of the Salzburg slate Alps to 1480. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In the Salzburg slate Alps the firm begins lending to mine owners who are always short of cash and never short of ore. Jakob works out the form that will hold for forty years: the loan is not repaid in coin but in Kuxe, shares in the pit, and in the right to the metal that comes out of it. The lender stops being a creditor and becomes an owner. Silver goes down the valley to Augsburg and credit goes back up it. The mine owners get the cash that keeps their shafts working, at Gastein and at Schladming both.
suggested_refs: Kuxe, the share in a mining pit, and the conversion of unsecured princely debt into metal rights
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Innsbruck, the factory at twenty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deutsche Biographie gives him the leadership of the Innsbruck factory from 1485, two years before the Venetian residence ends. The chronology pool also carries an 1487 'return from Venice' framed as a leadership marker; the two cannot both be the first, and 1485 is used here. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: He takes charge of the Innsbruck office two years before his Venetian residence formally ends, which means the young man still learning in the Fondaco is already running the branch that matters most. Innsbruck is where Tyrolean silver is counted and where Archduke Sigismund, called the Rich in Coin, borrows against it. Sigismund's court spends faster than his mountains produce. Every advance the Fuggers make him is secured on ore not yet dug. The archduke signs; the mountain owes.
suggested_refs: The Fugger factor's office at Innsbruck and the debts of Archduke Sigismund of Tyrol
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Schwaz, all the silver of the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deutsche Biographie states that by 1488 all silver production at Schwaz is handled by the Fugger firm, and the Fugger Foundation's chronology concurs, though that page could not be opened directly on the first pass and reaches this file through secondary compilation. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Schwaz is the richest silver district in Europe, and by this year every ounce of its production passes through Fugger hands. The firm advances against the ore, takes the output, and sells it where the price stands highest: down the Inn to Hall to be struck into coin, over the passes to Venice to be traded. One house in a Swabian free city now stands between the mountain and the mint. Under the Falkenstein, thousands of men work the galleries by candlelight, fighting water the drainage wheels cannot lift fast enough.
suggested_refs: The Falkenstein galleries at Schwaz and the Hall mint downstream of them
sources: Fugger Foundation chronology, as reported in secondary compilation

stops.name: Frankfurt, the fair and the archduke's heir
stops.date_confidence: traditional. The Fugger Foundation gives a first meeting with Maximilian I at a Frankfurt fair in 1489; the dossier calls the dating traditionally given rather than firmly documented. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At the Frankfurt fair, tradition says, the Augsburg merchant and the king of the Romans meet for the first time. Maximilian of Habsburg is thirty, magnificent, permanently insolvent, and about to inherit Tyrol. Jakob Fugger is thirty, unshowy, and holds paper on the man Maximilian is about to inherit it from. Neither will do without the other again for thirty years, and every campaign the emperor fancies will be paid on Fugger credit and secured on somebody's mine. The 1489 dating is traditional; no document fixes the meeting to that fair.
suggested_refs: The Frankfurt autumn fair as the Empire's clearing house for credit as well as goods
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Innsbruck, Sigismund gives up the county
stops.date_confidence: attested for the abdication and the transfer of debts: en.wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger', 16 March 1490. Fugger's personal presence at the act is not documented; he had run the Innsbruck factory for five years and held the paper that made the transfer necessary.
stops.campa: Archduke Sigismund, sunk in debt to the Fuggers and to half the merchants of Swabia, hands the county of Tyrol to his cousin Maximilian, who takes the obligations with the land and promises the Augsburgers repayment. A creditor's claim on a bankrupt prince converts, in one afternoon, into a claim on the Empire's next emperor, and the silver of Schwaz stands behind it either way. Sigismund lives on with a pension. Maximilian takes the land, the debt, and the silver that will have to service it.
suggested_refs: The 1490 transfer of Tyrol from Sigismund to Maximilian, with the assumption of Sigismund's debts

stops.name: Augsburg, Ulrich Fugger and Brothers
stops.date_confidence: attested for the constitution of the firm in 1494, which en.wikipedia describes as becoming one of the first open trading companies in Europe. Jakob's contribution of 15,552 guilders under the first agreement is a reconstruction, resting on the Fugger Foundation's partnership-record review rather than a document seen. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate inherited from the atlas's canonical Fugger-house pin.
stops.campa: The brothers put the house on paper. Ulrich Fugger and Brothers of Augsburg fixes shares, duties, and the term of the partnership between Ulrich, Georg, and Jakob, an instrument later called one of the first open trading companies in Europe. Jakob's own stake at the first agreement is put at 15,552 guilders, a figure that rests on the firm's partnership records rather than on the deed itself. Ulrich's name stands first because Ulrich is eldest. Every decision that grows the capital from here is Jakob's.
suggested_refs: The 1494 partnership agreement of Ulrich Fugger and Brothers of Augsburg, with its schedule of shares
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

segments.name: Copper, Pepper, and the Ends of the Earth

stops.name: Kraków, the partner who knows the water
stops.date_confidence: attested for the partnership with Johann (Jan) Thurzo the Elder, dated 1494-1495 across the sources; the Fugger Foundation gives the copper company itself as founded in 1495. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Johann Thurzo of Kraków knows how to get water out of a mine, which in Upper Hungary is the whole problem: the copper is there, the shafts flood, and the Hungarian owners have neither the pumps nor the capital. Fugger has the capital and a selling network running from Danzig to Lisbon. They put the two halves together, on a contract the sources date to 1494 or to 1495 depending which is read. Thurzo's son marries a Fugger niece. A Fugger nephew marries a Thurzo daughter.
suggested_refs: The Fugger-Thurzo contract of 1495 and the intermarriage that bound the two houses
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Neusohl, the copper works
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fugger Foundation dates the copper company to 1495, centred on Neusohl, today Banska Bystrica. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: At Neusohl in the Carpathian foothills the joint concern becomes one of the largest integrated metal enterprises in Europe: drainage engines, smelters, and the Saiger process that pulls the silver hidden inside Hungarian copper out of it with lead. Copper goes north by cart to Danzig and by water to Antwerp, south to Venice, west to Lisbon where it is loaded for India. The silver comes out as a by-product of the copper and pays for the running of the works, the drainage engines included.
suggested_refs: The Saiger process for separating silver from argentiferous copper, industrialized at Neusohl
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Fuggerau, the furnaces named for the family
stops.date_confidence: attested, with coordinate and date both corrected on verification. de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerau', places the works near Arnoldstein at 46.5481 / 13.6935, some 15 km west-southwest of Villach, and dates the build from 1495; the first pass gave Villach's own centre and 'early 1500s'. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Below Arnoldstein in Carinthia the family builds itself a town: smelting furnaces, a hammer mill, a brass foundry, and a works casting cannon, all fed by silver-bearing copper coming down from Hungary and Tyrol. They call it Fuggerau. It runs for half a century on ground that had been the monastery's, and the family name stays on the place. The Fuggers quit Hungarian mining in 1547, and in 1570 the site is sold back to the monastery of Arnoldstein for two thousand five hundred gulden.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerau works near Arnoldstein: furnaces, hammer mill, brass foundry, cannon works, 1495-1570

stops.name: Augsburg, marriage to Sibylle Arzt
stops.date_confidence: the date and the marriage are given by en.wikipedia and corroborated by the Fugger Foundation, but the pool tags this claim as reconstruction rather than attested; treated here as well transmitted, not as a document read. The claim that he held no Augsburg civic office is from Encyclopedia.com.
stops.campa: At thirty-eight he marries Sibylle Arzt, daughter of an Augsburg patrician family, and by that marriage enters the caste that governs the city. He never takes an office in it. Encyclopedia.com notes the point plainly: no post in Augsburg's government, then or afterward, despite the wealth and the Habsburg connection. He does not need the town hall and the town hall knows it. The marriage brings him standing and no children. When the will is read in 1525 it names a nephew.
suggested_refs: The Augsburg Herrenstube and the patrician society Sibylle Arzt's family belonged to
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Lisbon, the pepper contract
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia and the Fugger Foundation date the Lisbon establishment to 1503 and the Casa da India trading permission with it. The 1505-1506 India fleet subscription of about 3,000 guilders is attested separately and is folded into this stop. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The firm opens a factor's house at Lisbon and obtains from the Casa da Índia the right to trade pepper, spices, pearls, and gems. Two years later Fugger money rides with Augsburg, Nuremberg, and Genoese partners in a Portuguese fleet bound for the Malabar coast, about three thousand guilders of it. The books for all of it are kept in Augsburg and settled on the Tagus. Hungarian copper goes out in the holds, because India will take copper for pepper.
suggested_refs: The Casa da India and the German merchant subscription to the 1505-1506 Portuguese India fleet
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Rome, the guard that came down from the mountains
stops.date_confidence: the founding of the Swiss Guard under Julius II in 1506 is independently well documented; the Fugger firm's part in recruiting and transporting the first contingent rests on the crawled dossier's Curial-finance chronology and was not independently re-verified. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Julius II wants Swiss pikemen, and the Swiss want paying in advance, which is a problem that arrives at a banking house rather than a chancery. The Fugger company helps raise and move the first company of the papal guard to Rome. Beside the copper and the pepper it is a small piece of business, and it says plainly what the firm now is: a private house in a Swabian city that can put soldiers at a pope's door and ships on the Indian Ocean out of one ledger. The guard's founding in 1506 is documented on its own. The Fugger part in moving the first contingent rests on a single chronology and was not checked further.
suggested_refs: The founding of the Pontifical Swiss Guard under Julius II, 1506
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Rome, the papal mint
stops.date_confidence: attested for the span 1508 to 1515: en.wikipedia, 'Fugger', states that from 1508 to 1515 they leased the Roman mint. The first pass gave 'c.1508-1524, with interruptions', which is overstated and is corrected here. The exact mint-building coordinate remains unverified and is approximate. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: From 1508 the Fuggers lease the mint of Rome and strike the pope's coin for seven years, paying for repairs to the building out of their own money and working alongside the Curia's engravers. The Roman branch already moves Curial funds north, dispensations south, and indulgence receipts wherever they are owed. Now it makes the coin as well, and a merchant house of the Empire holds the die that stamps the keys of Saint Peter. The accounts for the papal mint are kept on the Weinmarkt in Augsburg, in double entry, in a hand learned at Venice. The lease runs out in 1515.
suggested_refs: The lease of the Roman Zecca to the Fugger firm, 1508-1515

stops.name: Kirchberg an der Iller, a county bought outright
stops.date_confidence: attested for date and price: en.wikipedia and Deutsche Biographie both give 15 July 1507 and about 50,000 guilders, with the Historisches Lexikon Bayerns cited in the pool for the same. Coordinate corrected to de.wikipedia's for the town, 48.1322 / 10.0806; the first pass had 48.1167 / 10.1167, about 3.5 km off.
stops.campa: Maximilian, wanting an Italian expedition and having no money, sells Jakob Fugger the county of Kirchberg together with the lordships of Weißenhorn, Wullenstetten, and Pfaffenhofen, for about fifty thousand guilders. The merchant becomes a landed lord with courts, tolls, and subjects. The emperor gets the money for his campaign into Italy. From here the man is no longer only a creditor of princes: he holds land in fee, by purchase, on a deed dated the fifteenth of July.
suggested_refs: The 1507 sale of the County of Kirchberg and its lordships, financing Maximilian's Italian expedition

stops.name: Weißenhorn, the town in the account book
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1507 acquisition (Fugger Foundation, which also records the later palace). The attribution of the town's quiet in 1525 to Fugger support for its textile trade is given without date in the pool and is a traditional explanation rather than a documented one. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Weißenhorn comes with the county and becomes the family's Swabian seat: a walled market town of weavers whose cloth the firm buys and sells on across the Empire. A Fugger palace goes up inside the walls in time. When the countryside rises in 1525 and burns its way across Swabia, Weißenhorn stays quiet, and the reason given afterward is that the lord who owns it has kept its looms in work. What lordship amounts to in this town is a standing order for fustian, and the explanation is the town's own, not a document of 1525.
suggested_refs: The Fugger palace at Weissenhorn and the town's weaving trade under Fugger lordship
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Augsburg, the chapel contracted at St Anna
stops.date_confidence: attested and sharpened by de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerkapelle': contract 4 April 1509, papal confirmation 19 November 1509, built 1509/10 to 1512 with the cartouches carrying MDXII, consecrated 17 January 1518. Coordinate corrected to de.wikipedia's for St Anna, 48.3678 / 10.8953; the first pass had 10.8974.
stops.campa: He contracts for a burial chapel at the west end of the Carmelite church of St Anna, for himself and for Ulrich and Georg, and has it built on Venetian and Roman models: barrel vault, marble reliefs, four epitaph panels, an organ case in seven parts. Dürer supplies designs, Burgkmair and Breu paint, Adolf Daucher carves. It is called the first Renaissance church interior on German soil. He is fifty, has no heir, and is building the room he will be looked at in.
suggested_refs: The Fugger Chapel at St Anna, Augsburg: contract 1509, consecration 17 January 1518
Duerer's designs and Adolf Daucher's carving for the chapel
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Augsburg, the last brother
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fugger Foundation records Georg's death in 1506 and Ulrich's in 1510, after which Jakob assumes sole leadership and responsibility for the whole firm. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinate inherited from the atlas's canonical Fugger-house pin.
stops.campa: Georg is four years dead and now Ulrich is dead too, and a partnership of brothers becomes a partnership of one. Jakob takes the whole firm: the Tyrolean silver, the Hungarian copper, the Roman mint, the Lisbon pepper, the debts of an emperor. He is fifty-one. Nephews are brought in and trained under him but never beside him. The shares are his and the decisions are his, and he answers to no partner and to no council in Augsburg. He runs it alone for the next fifteen years.
suggested_refs: The deaths of Georg Fugger (1506) and Ulrich Fugger (1510) and the concentration of the firm in Jakob's hands
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Augsburg, raised to the nobility
stops.date_confidence: attested for 8 May 1511: en.wikipedia, Deutsche Biographie, and the Fugger Foundation all carry the elevation to imperial nobility. The grant is an imperial act rather than a ceremony fixed to a place; the stop is set at his own city.
stops.campa: Maximilian raises him to the imperial nobility. The grant is paper, and the paper is the point: a man whose forebears entered Augsburg as village weavers, and whose father only crossed into the merchants' guild, now holds arms from the emperor's own hand. Three years later there is another patent and a higher one, signed by the same emperor, who owes him more by then than he did in 1511. On the shield, quartered and requartered as the family climbs, the lily stands on gold and blue.
suggested_refs: The Fugger von der Lilie arms and the patent of imperial nobility of 8 May 1511
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Augsburg, the Fuggerhäuser on the Weinmarkt
stops.date_confidence: attested for a build period of 1512 to 1515 with a later expansion in 1523 (Fugger Foundation; de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerhaeuser'). Coordinate conflict left standing rather than resolved: this file inherits the atlas's existing pin for the Fugger townhouse on the Maximilianstrasse, 48.36778 / 10.89528, while de.wikipedia gives 48.3658 / 10.8989 for the building, about 250 m away. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: On the Weinmarkt he builds a house that is also an office, a bank, a warehouse, and a court: a painted facade on the street, four courtyards behind it, and the Damenhof with its arcades on slender columns, which Germany will call its first secular Renaissance building. Kings lodge here. Cardinals lodge here. The counting room and the state rooms share a staircase, so that a prince who has come to borrow climbs past the desks where his debt is written down.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerhaeuser on the Weinmarkt and the Damenhof courtyard, built 1512-1515, expanded 1523
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Augsburg, imperial count
stops.date_confidence: attested for 17 July 1514 (en.wikipedia; Fugger Foundation). The claim that he is the first German merchant ever raised to that rank is credited in the pool to the Neue Deutsche Biographie, which was not consulted directly.
stops.campa: Three years after the patent of nobility Maximilian makes him an imperial count, a rank held by men whose families have sat on their land since the Hohenstaufen. The German national biography records him as the first German merchant ever raised to it, a claim that runs to that work and was not checked against another. Behind the grant there is no lineage and no service in the field. There is a ledger, and an emperor who has run out of ways to pay that do not cost him something he would rather keep.
suggested_refs: The patent of 17 July 1514 raising Jakob Fugger to Imperial Count
Neue Deutsche Biographie, entry on Jakob Fugger, for the first-merchant claim
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Augsburg, an archbishopric on credit
stops.date_confidence: attested: en.wikipedia gives the loan of about 20,000 guilders to Albrecht of Brandenburg for the papal dispensations required to hold Mainz alongside his other sees, with repayment structured through indulgence revenue. The transaction runs between Mainz and Rome; it is placed here at the firm's own house, because the Fugger side of it was transacted from Augsburg and Jakob's presence at Mainz is not documented. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Albrecht of Brandenburg wants Mainz while already holding Magdeburg and Halberstadt, which requires a dispensation, which requires money in Rome. The Fuggers advance him about twenty thousand guilders. Repayment is arranged out of the indulgence preached across his provinces for the building of St Peter's, with a Fugger agent standing beside the chest as the coins go in: half to Rome, half to the creditor. The theology of the arrangement is not the firm's department. Three years later a friar at Wittenberg writes ninety-five theses against the preaching of it.
suggested_refs: The 1514 Fugger loan to Albrecht of Brandenburg and the indulgence collection that serviced it
Johannes Eck's 1515 Bologna disputation on five-percent commercial deposit returns, sponsored by Fugger against the canon-law usury ban

segments.name: The Sudden Illness and the Hearing in His Own House

stops.name: Augsburg, ground broken for the Fuggerei
stops.date_confidence: attested for construction begun in 1516 (en.wikipedia; Fugger Foundation), with 52 houses standing by 1523. Coordinate corrected: the two lenses of the research pool disagreed with each other, giving 48.3729 / 10.9029 and 48.3667 / 10.9022, and both were wrong; de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerei', gives 48.3688 / 10.9041. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In the Jakobervorstadt, on ground the firm buys up house by house, masons begin a walled settlement of small identical dwellings for the poor of Augsburg: two rooms below, two above, a door of one's own, a gate shut at night. Fifty-two houses by 1523, one of them kept back for the administration. The rent is one Rhenish guilder a year and three prayers daily for the founders. The terms are drawn like any other contract the house makes, and they are drawn to run in perpetuity.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerei in the Jakobervorstadt: 52 houses, 102 dwellings, built 1516-1523
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Dillingen an der Donau, the sudden illness
stops.date_confidence: attested for the episode: the Fugger Foundation's fact-check page on the 1517 Dillingen visit gives the sole direct record as a letter of the canon Bernhard Adelmann von Adelmannsfelden dated 19 July 1517. The cause is a reconstruction and undeterminable; the Foundation's own conclusion is that natural illness, food poisoning, and deliberate attack cannot be distinguished. Poison rumours were later noted by Goetz von Poelnitz, whose biography was not read.
stops.campa: Visiting the newly consecrated prince-bishop Christoph von Stadion at Dillingen, Fugger and the provost of Bamberg are taken violently ill at the same hour. One letter, written by a canon on the nineteenth of July, is everything the record contains. He recovers. Augsburg talks: bad fish, bad water, or somebody's enemy paying a cook. No contemporary source names a poison, a hand, or a reason, and five centuries later the family's own foundation concludes the question cannot be settled.
suggested_refs: Bernhard Adelmann von Adelmannsfelden's letter of 19 July 1517, the sole direct record of the Dillingen illness
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'Fact check: Jakob Fugger's visit to Dillingen in 1517'

stops.name: Augsburg, the pope's grant at St Moritz
stops.date_confidence: attested that Leo X issued a document granting Fugger patronage rights connected to St Moritz in Augsburg in 1517 (en.wikipedia). Gap declared: the research pool supplies no verified coordinate for St Moritz, so this stop uses the city pin rather than the church's. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Leo X issues a document granting the Fuggers rights of patronage at the church of St Moritz. It is one more piece of a package Jakob is assembling in his own city: the burial chapel at St Anna, the almshouses in the Jakober suburb, and now an endowed preachership whose holder he will name. The man who has been moving the Curia's money for thirty years knows which office issues which paper and what each one costs. Four years later all three are bound into a single charter.
suggested_refs: The St Moritz preaching endowment, later bound into the 1521 foundation charter

stops.name: Augsburg, the Fuggerhäuser: Cajetan and the monk
stops.date_confidence: attested for the venue: Cardinal Cajetan lodges in the Fugger house during the imperial diet and examines Luther there over three days in October 1518. Jakob Fugger's own participation is not attested, and his biographer Goetz von Poelnitz argues he kept away. Day within October unknown, defaulted to 01. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from martin_luther.journey.json.
stops.campa: Cardinal Cajetan takes his lodging in the Fuggerhäuser for the imperial diet, and for three days in October the ablest Thomist in Europe examines an Augustinian friar from Wittenberg in the owner's own state rooms. Cajetan wants one word. Martin Luther will not say it, and leaves the city at night through a small gate. The house's owner is not recorded in the room. The indulgence they are arguing about was preached to service his loan, and his agent counted the takings.
suggested_refs: The three-day examination of Luther by Cardinal Cajetan in the Fuggerhaeuser, October 1518
sources: martin_luther.journey.json, stop 'Augsburg, three days before Cajetan'

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the crown assembled in guilders
stops.date_confidence: attested for the election of Charles V as king of the Romans and for the concentration of the funds at Frankfurt (Deutsche Biographie: over 850,000 concentrated there). Cross-source discrepancy left standing: en.wikipedia's Jakob Fugger page dates the election 28 July, which the independently consulted dossier flags as a documented error for 28 June; 28 June is used here. The Fugger share is given as roughly 543,000 in one lens and over 500,000 in another. Jakob's own presence at Frankfurt is not documented; the firm's agents and the firm's money were there.
stops.campa: Seven electors sit at Frankfurt with three candidates before them: Charles of Spain, Francis of France, and Henry of England. The votes are bought openly and in writing, against bills payable in Augsburg. Of roughly eight hundred and fifty thousand guilders promised, the Fugger house finds about five hundred and forty-three thousand. Charles is elected unanimously on the twenty-eighth of June. He is nineteen, and he rules Spain, the Netherlands, Austria, and the Indies. The bills fall due in Augsburg and go unpaid for years.
suggested_refs: The electoral bills of 1519 payable at Augsburg, and the Fugger share of the election spend

stops.name: Augsburg, the name in the pamphlets
stops.date_confidence: attested that Luther's An den christlichen Adel deutscher Nation of 1520 calls for a bridle on the Fuggers; the passage is in the treatise itself and is quoted here from the English Wikisource rendering. Correction recorded: de.wikipedia's modernized German gives the singular, 'dem Fugger', and frames the line as a personal attack on Jakob by name, which the text does not support, and its own footnote for the line is Aloys Schulte, Die Fugger in Rom 1495-1523 (Leipzig, 1904), not Luther. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The pamphlet presses of the Empire have found a name for what is wrong with money, and it is his. Martin Luther, addressing the Christian nobility of the German nation, asks how it is possible that in a single man's lifetime such a heap should be piled up lawfully, and says a bridle ought to be found for the Fuggers and companies like them. Ulrich von Hutten works the same seam harder and dirtier. Fugger answers none of it in print. He goes on lending to the emperor who will shortly try Luther at Worms.
stops.quote: Doubtless we should also find some bridle for the Fuggers and similar companies.
stops.quote_source: Martin Luther, An den christlichen Adel deutscher Nation, 1520; English Wikisource rendering, Harvard Classics vol. 36 (1910)
suggested_refs: Luther, An den christlichen Adel deutscher Nation (1520), on monopoly and the trading companies
Aloys Schulte, Die Fugger in Rom 1495-1523 (Leipzig, 1904)
sources: English Wikisource, 'Address to the Christian Nobility of the German Nation'
de.wikipedia, 'An den christlichen Adel deutscher Nation'

stops.name: Schwaz, the chronicler's reckoning
stops.date_confidence: the chronicler is anonymous even in the citation, and the passage is undated beyond 'early sixteenth century'; the 1520 date orders the segment only. Source traced on verification to Eike Eberhard Unger, Die Fugger in Hall i.T. (Tuebingen, 1967), reported via de.wikipedia; the monograph itself was not read. The German as transmitted is in modern orthography, so it is a reported text and not a verbatim period quotation.
stops.campa: A Tyrolean who is never named writes down what everyone in the valley can already see: that in this country everything worth money is pledged, that the Fuggers of Augsburg hold the great estate at Schwaz, and that they draw two hundred thousand gulden a year out of it. Two hundred thousand gulden a year leaves the valley in carts, and nobody in Tyrol disputes the figure. What the valley disputes is who ought to be drawing it. The passage comes down in modern spelling, through a monograph of 1967, from a chronicler nobody has ever put a name to.
stops.quote: in diesem Land ist Alles versetzt, was Geld beträgt, die Fugger von Augsburg haben das große Gut zu Schwaz inne und ziehen daraus jährlich 200.000 Gulden
stops.quote_source: An unnamed Tyrolean chronicler, reported in Eike Eberhard Unger, Die Fugger in Hall i.T. (Tübingen, 1967), as quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger'; modern orthography, reported text rather than verbatim period wording
suggested_refs: Eike Eberhard Unger, Die Fugger in Hall i.T. (Tuebingen, 1967)

stops.name: Augsburg, the foundation charter
stops.date_confidence: attested for 23 August 1521 (Fugger Foundation; en.wikipedia), binding the St Anna burial chapel, the St Moritz preachership, and the Fuggerei into one endowment, funded by a 10,000-florin account in memory of Georg and Ulrich (Encyclopedia.com). Citation chain for the quoted charter wording declared weak: the text is verified verbatim on de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerei', but that article's footnote is a tourism website rather than a scholarly edition or the Fugger archive, and no better edition was found. The archival original was not consulted.
stops.campa: On the twenty-third of August he signs one charter binding three things into one: the burial chapel at St Anna, the preachership at St Moritz, and the houses in the Jakobervorstadt. Ten thousand florins are set aside in memory of Georg and Ulrich, and the interest carries all three in perpetuity. The houses, the charter says, are to be lent for God's sake to pious poor day labourers and craftsmen and burghers and residents of this city of Augsburg, with no favour, bribe, or gift looked for.
stops.quote: Namlich so sollen soliche hewser Fromen Armen taglönern und handtwerckern und burgern und inwonern dieser stadt Augsburg, die es notturftig sein und am besten angelegt ist, umb gottes willen gelichen und darin weder schankung muet und gab nit angesehen
stops.quote_source: Stiftungsbrief of the Fuggerei, 23 August 1521, as quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerei'; archival edition not consulted
suggested_refs: The Stiftungsbrief of 23 August 1521 and the 10,000-florin endowment in memory of Georg and Ulrich Fugger
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'Jakob Fugger, the world's most successful philanthropist'

stops.name: Augsburg, fifty-two houses standing
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Fugger Foundation records 52 houses constructed by 1523, and de.wikipedia, 'Fuggerei', gives 52 houses with 102 dwellings built 1516-1523, one house reserved for administration, and 67 houses with 140 apartments today. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The settlement is finished: fifty-two houses, a hundred and two dwellings, a chapel, and a gate that shuts at nightfall. The tenant must be a needy Catholic citizen of Augsburg who has fallen into want through no fault, and must say three prayers a day for the souls of the founders. The rent stays at one guilder a year. Five hundred years later the rent is still one guilder and people still live there, in sixty-seven houses now, a hundred and forty apartments.
suggested_refs: The Fuggerei's conditions of residence: Catholic, Augsburg-born, needy without fault, three daily prayers
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Nuremberg, the Diet and the word monopoly
stops.date_confidence: attested for the proceedings, which ran across the Diets of Nuremberg in 1522 and 1523 and were suspended in 1524 with no criminal conviction after Charles V ordered them stopped; the Fugger Foundation records the 1523 intervention in the trade restrictions debate. Jakob's personal attendance is not documented; the firm was represented and he intervened by letter. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The imperial estates and the fiscal officers of the Empire put the great trading companies on trial at Nuremberg, and the charge is monopoly: that three or four houses in Swabia hold the copper, the silver, and the spices of Europe and set the price of all of them. The Fuggers are named first because the Fuggers are largest. Charles V orders the proceedings stopped. The case is suspended in 1524, nobody is convicted, and the word monopoly stays attached to the name.
suggested_refs: The monopoly proceedings against the great trading companies at the Diets of Nuremberg, 1522-1524
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'The most important firm of its time'

stops.name: Augsburg, the letter to the emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the letter of 1523 (en.wikipedia); the German text is as given in Franz Herre, Die Fugger in ihrer Zeit (Augsburg, 2000), quoted with citation on de.wikipedia. The dossier flags that the wording should be checked against the archival edition before extended quotation, and that check was not made, so the punctuation and ellipsis are secondary-source transmission of a genuine letter. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: With the monopoly case running at Nuremberg and his loans unrepaid, he writes to Charles V and does not trouble with courtesy or with the usual approaches. It is well known, he says, and plain as day, that Your Imperial Majesty could not have obtained the Roman crown without my doing. Then he asks for his money, in the same paragraph, as a man asks a debtor. No rebuke comes back. Charles orders the proceedings at Nuremberg stopped, and what the letter had to do with that order is not on record.
stops.quote: Es ist auch wissentlich und liegt am Tage, dass Eure Kaiserliche Majestät die römische Krone ohne mein Zutun nicht hätte erlangen können
stops.quote_source: Jakob Fugger to Emperor Charles V, 1523; German text as given in Franz Herre, Die Fugger in ihrer Zeit (Augsburg, 2000), quoted in de.wikipedia, 'Jakob Fugger'
suggested_refs: Franz Herre, Die Fugger in ihrer Zeit (Augsburg, 2000), for the German text of the 1523 letter

stops.name: Almadén, the mercury of the military orders
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Maestrazgos lease taking effect 1 January 1525, giving the Fuggers the revenues and properties of the orders of Santiago, Calatrava and Alcantara, with the Almaden mines among them. Discrepancy left standing: the Fugger Foundation dates a quicksilver mining rights grant to 1523, while the dossier dates the broader lease to 1 January 1525; the two may describe different stages of one arrangement.
stops.campa: Charles V, unable to pay, leases his creditor the revenues of the Spanish military orders: Santiago, Calatrava, Alcántara, their commanderies, their pastures, their tolls, and the cinnabar of Almadén, where the mercury is dug that pulls silver out of its ore. The crusading orders of Castile stand pledged to a merchant in Swabia as security for a German election. Jakob Fugger will be dead within the year, and the lease will run in his family's hands for most of the century.
suggested_refs: The Maestrazgos lease of 1 January 1525: the revenues of Santiago, Calatrava and Alcantara pledged to the Fuggers
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Weißenhorn, the rebel peasants
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance, weak in wording. The source chain for Fugger calling the rebels lazy rabble who wanted to be rich without exerting themselves runs only to Greg Steinmetz, Der reichste Mann der Weltgeschichte (Munich, 2016), p. 306, itself the German translation of an English book; no primary letter or chronicle stands behind the German words, which are a translator's rendering, so they are not set here as period German. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: Swabia rises. Bands of peasants burn abbeys and castles across the country he now holds land in, and the Twelve Articles are read out in market squares from Memmingen to the Danube. Fugger, sixty-six and lord of Kirchberg, calls them lazy rabble who want to be rich without exerting themselves. The words come down through a modern biographer and no further; no letter of his and no chronicle of the war carries them. Weißenhorn does not rise, and the looms there keep working.
suggested_refs: Greg Steinmetz, Der reichste Mann der Weltgeschichte (Munich, 2016), p. 306, terminus of the 'lazy rabble' attribution

stops.name: Schwaz, the miners stop working
stops.date_confidence: attested: habsburger.net, 'Anti-Fuggerians: mines', records the 1525 Tyrolean miners' strike over hazardous conditions, unreliable pay and Fugger mining privileges, and Archduke Ferdinand I's threats followed by his leaving the Fugger rights in place. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: The men in the Falkenstein galleries stop work. They want reliable pay, safer shafts, and an end to the privileges of the one Augsburg house that has handled every ounce of Schwaz silver for thirty-seven years. Archduke Ferdinand, holding Tyrol for his brother the emperor, threatens punishment, listens, and leaves the Fugger rights exactly where they were. It is the same season as the peasant risings in the lowlands. Nothing about the privileges changes.
suggested_refs: The 1525 Tyrolean miners' strike and the anti-Fugger agitation in the Inn valley

stops.name: Buda, the house is stormed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and uncorroborated. The storming of the Fugger house at Buda amid the Upper Hungarian copper dispute appears only in the crawled dossier; the habsburger.net page on the 1525 anti-Fugger mining unrest covers Tyrol and does not mention Buda or this episode at all. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01.
stops.campa: In Hungary the copper concern has made enemies at court, and the story that reaches Augsburg is that the Fugger house at Buda has been broken open, its money and goods seized, and a submission agreement pushed at the firm's factors. Fugger refuses to sign and answers with a blockade of the trade instead. The account rests on one line of transmission, and no Hungarian source reachable here carries it. Something happened at Buda that year. What, exactly, is not established.
suggested_refs: The Upper Hungarian copper dispute of 1525 and the Fugger factory at Buda

stops.name: Augsburg, the second testament
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction for the date. Anton Fugger's designated succession is independently well documented (Fugger Foundation; en.wikipedia); the 28 December dating of the second and final testament rests on the dossier. The quoted reply is reported by Max Weber, who attaches no date and no death context and names the addressee only as a business associate who urged him to retire; it is placed here as a reported remark, not a documented deathbed utterance, and not as Fugger's own pen.
stops.campa: Two days before he dies he signs the second and final testament, disposing of the business and naming his nephew Anton to lead it. There are no children to provide for. Long before, when an associate told him he had earned enough and might retire and leave something for others to earn, he had answered that he was of quite another mind, and meant to go on gaining as long as he was able to gain. The sentence comes down through a report of an anecdote, not through a letter in his own hand.
stops.quote: er hätte viel einen anderen Sinn, wollte gewinnen, dieweil er könnte
stops.quote_source: Jakob Fugger's reply to a business associate urging him to retire, as reported by Max Weber, Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus (1904/05), section 'Der Geist des Kapitalismus'
suggested_refs: Max Weber, Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus (1904/05), which sets the Fugger reply against Benjamin Franklin
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'
Max Weber, Die protestantische Ethik und der Geist des Kapitalismus

stops.name: Augsburg, death in his own house
stops.date_confidence: attested: Deutsche Biographie gives death on 30 December 1525 at Augsburg; en.wikipedia adds the inventory figures and the naming of Anton as successor, and the Fugger Foundation corroborates the succession.
stops.campa: He dies on the thirtieth of December in the house on the Weinmarkt, sixty-six years old, two generations out of the weavers' guild of that same city. The inventory taken afterward puts the company's assets at about three million and fifty-eight guilders against liabilities of about eight hundred and sixty-seven thousand. Anton assumes the leadership the next morning, under authority his uncle had written out in advance. Charles V still owes him, and so does Ferdinand.
suggested_refs: The post-mortem inventory of 1525: assets c.3,000,058 guilders against liabilities c.867,797
sources: Fugger Foundation, fugger.de, 'History of the Fugger family since 1367'

stops.name: Augsburg, buried in the chapel he built
stops.date_confidence: attested for burial at St Anna (Deutsche Biographie: buried at Sankt Anna church in Augsburg). The exact day of interment is not given in the sources; 31 December orders the sequence only. The chapel's survival as Catholic property inside a Lutheran parish from 1548, and the removal of the choir-stall busts in 1848-1850, are attested by en.wikipedia and de.wikipedia and are the afterlife of an object he himself commissioned.
stops.campa: He is laid in the chapel at St Anna, under the marble he commissioned sixteen years earlier, beside Ulrich and Georg. In 1548 the church becomes Lutheran and the chapel does not: the family foundation keeps it Catholic, a Roman burial choir at the west end of a Protestant parish, and it stays that way. Three centuries later, in the secularization, the wooden portrait busts are carried out of its choir stalls and away to the museums of Berlin, and most of them burn in the war. Three survive.
suggested_refs: The Fugger Chapel's Catholic status inside Lutheran St Anna from 1548
The three surviving choir-stall busts from the Fugger Chapel, Bode-Museum, Berlin
